title: Performance trade-offs define a fundamental dental dichotomy in mammals.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and read the full 39-page supplementary PDF (5.3 MB) from the University of Liege repository ORBi, which contains the Materials and Methods and the captions for Data S1-S4. Probed the four data files on science.org (Data S1 specimen list .xlsx, Data S2 raw mechanical results .xlsx, Data S3 R script, Data S4 DIC .zip): all return HTTP 403 (blocked). Probed the MorphoSource project page 000792218 holding the 3D tooth meshes: blocked by an Anubis proof-of-work challenge, so no file listing or mesh count obtained. Europe PMC reports no open-access full text, no supplementary files, no accessions.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: All counts: 250 teeth, one per species (106 Feliformia, 111 Caniformia, 29 'creodonts', 4 Miacidae); 12 fixed landmarks plus 2,000 surface pseudo-landmarks per tooth; a subset of 45 real teeth plus 4 theoretical shapes 3D-printed and physically tested; 3 repeat trials per tooth for slicing and 3 for crushing; the measured variables (breakage load in newtons, displacement in mm, elastic slope, 0-6 tooth damage score, 0-9 bone damage score, puncture force) and their normalisation to 0-1. None of these numbers were confirmed against a file.

a1_downloadable.note: No data file could be retrieved. Data S1-S4 sit only on science.org and return HTTP 403; the 3D meshes sit on MorphoSource behind a bot challenge; and the paper itself states 'sharing restrictions apply to some' specimens, so the mesh set is only partially releasable even to a human with a browser. Checked by probing the URLs, not inferred.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: From the supplement's caption only: Data S2 'Carnassial_mechanical_data.xlsx' is described as the raw experimental results, so breakage load, slope and damage scores should be columns. Not verified in a file.

a3_inputs_present.note: The input is a 3D tooth mesh or its 2,012 landmark coordinates. The landmark coordinate matrix is not listed among Data S1-S4 (only a specimen list, mechanical results, an R script and digital-image-correlation ASCII files), and the meshes are on a separate, partly restricted repository. Checked against the supplement's file captions.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are explicit in the methods: force in newtons, displacement in mm, time in s, teeth scaled to 3 cm mesiodistal length; damage on stated 0-6 and 0-9 ordinal scales. Read in the paper's supplement, not in a file.

a5_enough_rows.note: Decisive failure. The mechanical performance label exists for only 49 teeth (45 real species plus 4 theoretical shapes), each tested in 3 repeats; the shape dataset is 250 species with one specimen each. Both are far under the ~1,500-row regression and ~400-row classification thresholds. Numbers read in the supplement.

a6_fits_laptop.note: 49 to 250 tooth meshes plus two small spreadsheets would be well under a gigabyte; estimated from counts, no file sizes seen.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cannot be checked at all: no file was retrievable, so paper, repository and download could not be compared. Recorded as unverifiable rather than as a disagreement.

a8_label_provenance.note: For the 49 printed teeth the label is a real physical measurement (good). But the paper's performance values for the other ~201 species are interpolated across the morphospace by the Morphoscape R package from those 49 points, so any species-level performance label would be another model's output computed from the same shape features used as input - circular by construction.

honest_claim_h3: With 49 physically tested teeth, the most a model could honestly claim is that tooth shape ranks slicing and crushing performance among a hand-picked 45 species sampled to span the morphospace - a sentence about 45 species, not about mammals.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the three-dimensional shape of a carnivore's flesh-slicing tooth to predict how well it slices meat and crushes bone.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one lower carnassial (the main shearing cheek tooth) described by 12 anatomical landmarks plus 2,000 evenly spread surface points. Only 49 teeth (45 real species, 4 theoretical shapes) have a measured performance value; 250 species have shape only.
plain_idea.predict: Two continuous performance scores: force and puncture depth when the 3D-printed tooth is driven into medical gelatin (slicing), and breakage load, elastic slope and damage scores when it is pressed onto a 3D-printed gazelle femur (crushing), measured on a Mark-10 testing frame.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Palaeontologists infer diet from fossil teeth by eye; a shape-to-performance predictor would let them score any scanned fossil tooth without printing and crushing it. Even a failure would quantify how much of mechanical performance 3D shape alone can explain.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: regress physically measured slicing and crushing performance on high-density 3D shape of mammalian carnassial teeth, then apply it to the 201 un-tested species and to new fossil scans. It dies on sample size (49 labelled teeth) and on data access (no file downloadable, meshes partly restricted by the authors).

effort.compute_note: No compute estimate made: Part A failed on sample size and data access, and no data file was retrievable to measure anything.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count how many teeth were physically tested rather than how many were scanned. The supplement says 45 real teeth plus 4 theoretical shapes - that one sentence kills the project in five minutes, before any download.

verdict_reason: Only 49 teeth carry a measured performance label (A5), performance for the other ~201 species is interpolated from those 49 by the authors' own landscape model (A8), and no data file is retrievable - science.org returns 403, MorphoSource is bot-blocked, and the authors state some meshes cannot be shared (A1, A3). Beautiful experiment, far too few labelled rows for machine learning.
